# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is established therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD). Landmark trials demonstrated that defibrillator implantation improves survival in high-risk populations, both in secondary prevention and in primary prevention. Unsustained ventricular tachycardia in patients with previous myocardial infarction and left ventricular dysfunction is associated with a high two-year mortality rate, and prophylactic therapy with an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator, as compared with conventional medical therapy, improves survival in this high-risk group [1]. The implantation of a defibrillator improves survival in patients with a prior myocardial infarction and advanced left ventricular dysfunction; thus, prophylactic implantation of a defibrillator is recommended in these patients [2]. For decades, transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) were the standard of care [3].

However, transvenous systems carry well-recognized risks. The defibrillator lead is the weakest part of the transvenous ICD system and a frequent cause of morbidity; lead dislodgement, cardiac perforation, pneumothorax and vascular injury are common early complications, while venous occlusion, tricuspid valve dysfunction, lead fracture and insulation failure are later complications [4]. At 10 years post-implant, the risk of lead failure can be as high as 25% in patients with a transvenous ICD [5].

## Concept and Development

The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was conceived to eliminate intravascular hardware. The S-ICD was developed to overcome the risk of lead-related complications associated with the TV-ICD, and in contrast to the TV-ICD, the S-ICD is a completely extrathoracic device [6]. The development of an entirely subcutaneous ICD was motivated initially by special circumstances where a traditional endovascular system was not practical, and it was first applied in the pediatric population, where congenital anatomic variation often precludes safe endocardial lead placement [7].

A trade-off is device size. Its extrathoracic design results in a generator twice the size of transvenous ICDs [8]. The S-ICD also lacks long-term bradycardia and antitachycardia pacing (ATP) capability, which limits eligibility in patients needing pacing or resynchronization [9].

## Sensing and Arrhythmia Discrimination

Because the S-ICD senses from a subcutaneous electrode array, novel detection algorithms were required. The START study compared the discrimination performance of subcutaneous and transvenous detection. The Subcutaneous versus Transvenous Arrhythmia Recognition Testing study was a prospective, multicenter trial comparing simulated sensing performances of the S-ICD system with single- and dual-chamber transvenous ICD systems [10]. Specificity for supraventricular arrhythmias was significantly better for the S-ICD system compared to the composite of transvenous devices, while ventricular arrhythmia detection was excellent across all systems [11].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The pivotal investigational device exemption (IDE) trial established initial safety and efficacy. The most frequent complications associated with ICDs involve the transvenous leads; an S-ICD was developed as an alternative system, and this study evaluated the safety and effectiveness of the S-ICD System for the treatment of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [12]. A pooled analysis of the IDE study and EFFORTLESS registry confirmed two-year outcomes [13]. Real-world registry data accumulated through EFFORTLESS, which was developed to defibrillate ventricular arrhythmias avoiding drawbacks of transvenous leads, and the global registry collected outcomes in 985 patients during 5-year follow-up [14]. Early registry results [15] and long-term 5-year outcomes [16] demonstrated durable efficacy. Initial clinical experience in a large Dutch cohort [17] and reports in children and adults [18] also informed practice, while inappropriate shocks emerged as an important early concern [19].

## Randomized Comparisons

The PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized head-to-head comparison. In this trial, 849 patients with a class I or IIa indication for ICD therapy without the need for pacing were randomized to either S-ICD or TV-ICD therapy, and patients were followed for a median duration of 49.1 months [20]. In patients with an indication for an ICD but no indication for pacing, the subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD with respect to device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [20]. A prespecified secondary analysis examined complications in detail [21], and longer follow-up is being pursued in PRAETORIAN-XL to test for superiority. The PRAETORIAN-XL trial aims to investigate whether the S-ICD is superior to the TV-ICD with respect to device-related complications at 8-year follow-up [22].

The ATLAS trial enriched for younger and higher-risk patients. A composite of major lead-related outcomes had occurred in one patient who received an S-ICD and 12 who received a transvenous ICD by 6 months, a 92% relative reduction with the S-ICD [23]. Inappropriate shocks were numerically more frequent in the S-ICD group, with an annualized rate of 2.7%, than in the transvenous group at 1.7% [23]. A randomized substudy further showed that ICD leads affect the tricuspid valve and right ventricle, favoring subcutaneous leads [24].

## Refining Patient Selection and Outcomes

The UNTOUCHED trial addressed a sicker cohort. Because patients in previous S-ICD studies had fewer comorbidities and less left ventricular dysfunction, UNTOUCHED was designed to evaluate the inappropriate shock rate in a more typical, contemporary ICD population implanted with the S-ICD using standardized programming and enhanced discrimination algorithms, including primary prevention patients with ejection fraction ≤35% [25]. The trial reported one of the lowest inappropriate shock rates seen in ICD studies [25].

Optimal implant position is critical to defibrillation success. Suboptimal positioning of the S-ICD increases the defibrillation threshold and risk of conversion failure, prompting development of the PRAETORIAN score to evaluate implant position and predict defibrillation success [26], which was subsequently validated in the PRAETORIAN-DFT trial [27]. Postoperative pain and patient-reported outcomes have also been characterized in contemporary cohorts [28].

## Guidelines and Future Directions

Contemporary guidelines incorporate the S-ICD as an option for patients without pacing needs [29]. A major limitation—the absence of pacing—is being addressed through modular systems. A leadless pacemaker in wireless communication with a subcutaneous ICD exceeded performance goals for freedom from major complications, for communication between the leadless pacemaker and subcutaneous ICD, and for pacing thresholds at 6 months [30]. This modular concept may extend S-ICD eligibility by providing ATP and bradycardia pacing without transvenous leads.

## Conclusion

The S-ICD has matured from a niche device into a validated alternative to the TV-ICD for patients without a pacing indication, with randomized evidence supporting noninferiority for complications and superiority for lead-related harm. Ongoing trials and modular leadless innovations are poised to broaden its role in SCD prevention.
